title: Roundabouts: The Problem Is You
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss roundabouts: what they are (also called traffic circles, rotaries, gyratories), early history from Pierre L'Enfant's Washington D.C. circles and New York's Columbus Circle in 1905, the flawed yield rule of early rotaries fixed in Britain in 1966, US resistance and Eisenhower's interstate preference, design principles, roundabout variants (dog bone, dumbbell, hamburger, flower, turbo), safety statistics on conflict points and crash reductions, costs and fuel savings, driving tips, pop culture (European Vacation, Carmel Indiana's roundabout record, Swindon's Magic Roundabout), and closing with a listener-mail-free sign-off.

segments.title: Opening banter and roundabout enthusiasm
segments.summary: Hosts joke about working without producers, then discuss their shared dislike of drivers on phones and slow drivers, and their love of roundabouts, including a recent roundabout near Emory Village.

segments.title: What a roundabout is
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh define a roundabout as a circle placed at an intersection where traffic must go around a central island, also called a traffic circle, rotary, or gyratory, and describe its specific traits and how to navigate it, comparing it to a tiny circular expressway.

segments.title: Early history: Washington D.C. and Columbus Circle
segments.summary: Early circular traffic patterns appear in Washington D.C. through Pierre L'Enfant. The hosts say the first true traffic circle for cars was Columbus Circle in New York City in 1905, designed by Bill William Eno, followed by a British one-way gyratory in Letchworth Garden City.

segments.title: The backwards yield rule and the 1966 British fix
segments.summary: Early rotaries gave right of way to entering traffic, causing decades of congestion and crashes from the 1930s to mid-1950s. In 1966 Britain reversed the yield so circulating traffic had priority, cutting delays and raising capacity. The US abandoned rotaries, tearing some out, and its first modern roundabout came in Summerland, Nevada, in 1990.

segments.title: Why America resisted roundabouts
segments.summary: The hosts describe Eisenhower seeing Paris gridlock and German autobahns and favoring interstates, and a theory that British cooperative culture suited roundabouts while US culture is more confrontational. They note Ohio's 1980s opposition and the UK Roundabout Appreciation Society's view that traffic lights are fascist.

segments.title: Roundabout design principles
segments.summary: Five design characteristics: yield on entry with no signs inside, vehicles inside have right of way, pedestrians cross only at legs behind yield signs, no parking in the circulating roadway, and counterclockwise traffic around a central island. Smaller radius means slower speeds. Hosts discuss the Atlanta roundabout at a mall and neighborhood roundabouts.

segments.title: Roundabout variants and safety
segments.summary: Variants include dog bone, dumbbell, hamburger, flower with slip lanes, and turbo roundabouts with lane choice. Roundabouts have eight conflict points versus thirty-two at a four-way lighted intersection. A 2000 study of twenty-four US roundabouts found a 76 percent drop in injury crashes. Roundabouts also cost less to maintain and reduce fuel use and emissions.

segments.title: How to drive a roundabout and pop culture
segments.summary: Driving tips: slow down, yield to pedestrians and cyclists, look left, enter when clear, do not stop inside, use signals, and pick the correct lane in multi-lane roundabouts. The hosts then mention European Vacation, Jon Insands' three-and-a-half-hour drive around a dog bone roundabout in Carmel, Indiana, Carmel's roundabout count, and Swindon's Magic Roundabout.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts wrap up the episode, ask listeners to spread the word and leave reviews, mention the merch store and contact email, and sign off.
